payload.user_input: How does TLS 1.3 differ from TLS 1.2 in its handshake process?
payload.output: TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake from two round-trips to one (1-RTT) by combining the ClientHello and key-share into a single flight. It removes support for static RSA key exchange and legacy cipher suites such as CBC-mode ciphers, retaining only AEAD algorithms like AES-128-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. The server responds with its key-share, encrypted extensions, and finished message in one flight, allowing application data to flow after just one round-trip. TLS 1.3 also supports 0-RTT resumption, where cached pre-shared keys let clients send early data before the handshake completes, at the cost of reduced replay protection.
payload.context: TLS 1.3, defined in RFC 8446, redesigns the handshake to complete in a single round-trip (1-RTT) instead of the two round-trips required by TLS 1.2. The client sends a ClientHello message that includes supported cipher suites and one or more key-share entries (typically ECDHE). The server selects a cipher suite, responds with its own key-share, and derives handshake keys immediately. All cipher suites in TLS 1.3 use AEAD constructions; supported algorithms include AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges, CBC-mode ciphers, and MD5/SHA-1 hash functions are removed. A 0-RTT mode allows session resumption with pre-shared keys (PSK), enabling clients to send early application data in the first flight, though this data is not forward-secret and is susceptible to replay attacks.
